ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The aim of this work was to gain insights about the feasibility of chlorinated solvents removal through biostimulated and bioaugmented biological processes in laboratory-scale permeable reactive barriers (PRBs) under anaerobic and aerobic conditions. The experimental plant consisted of two Plexiglas cylindrical columns filled with silica sand and fed with real groundwater contaminated by chlorinated solvents (mainly 1,2-dichloroethane, 1,2-DCA, at a concentration of 20 mg l−1). Column A simulated a PRB containing poly-β-hydroxybutyrate (PHB) powder as electron donor and worked under anaerobic conditions; in Column B an inlet air flow rate ensured aerobic conditions. Both columns were inoculated with dechlorinating bacterial consortia obtained by enrichment cultures from the same contaminated groundwater. Results from Column A showed that PHB can be fermented and used as a slow-releasing carbon source for sustaining reductive dechlorination, as revealed by acetate production up to 267 mg l−1 and 100% 1,2-DCA removal. The microbial community detected in Column A at the end of the experimental period was mainly enriched in sulfate reducing bacteria that could act as both fermenting and dechlorinating agents. Column B showed a slight lower 1,2-DCA removal efficiency (98%) likely related to the establishment of aerobic (co)metabolic processes.

ce:section.ce:para: Chlorinated solvents are a subgroup of organ-halogen compounds belonging to the class of chlorinated aliphatic hydrocarbons. They have been widely used in various industrial sectors as degreasers, dry cleaning, and solvents in the chemical-pharmaceutical industry (Chang et al., 2017; Anam et al., 2019). However, these compounds pose significant environmental risk because of their poor solubility and degradability, and their high toxicity and carcinogenicity make them dangerous to human health (Yu et al., 2023). Improper handling and disposal practices often lead to their release into the environment, where they can contaminate various environmental matrices, especially the aquifers (APAT IRSA-CNR, 2003; Bradley, 2003; Majone et al., 2015; Pierro et al., 2016, 2017; Anam et al., 2019; Aulenta et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2023). Chlorinated solvents commonly found in the environment include 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA), 1,1,1-trichloroethane, carbon tetrachloride, methylene chloride, chloroform, tetrachloroethylene (PCE), and trichloroethylene (TCE). These compounds exhibit specific chemical-physical characteristics such as high vapor pressure, higher density than water and limited water solubility (Ajo-Franklin et al., 2006). As a result, when released in large quantities, they tend to form dense non-aqueous phase liquids (DNAPLs) and can rapidly percolate through unsaturated soils, reaching aquifers. Once in the aquifer, they settle at the impermeable bottom and disperse along the direction of water flow (Sleep and Sykes, 1989; Cohen and Mercer, 1993; Pierro et al., 2016).

Conventionally applied remediation processes, such as Pump & Treat (P&T), are ineffective to solve DNAPLs contamination. These treatments are often based on contaminant phase transfer, regardless of its effective degradation, and rarely allow to reach the low standard limits imposed by Regulations for water reinjection into the aquifers; therefore, the final destiny is often the discharge into surface water bodies (Starr and Cherry, 1994; Beretta, 2000; Majone, 2009). Currently, the interest is directed towards the development of new in situ remediation technologies, including permeable reactive barriers (PRBs) based on physical-chemical and biological processes (Majone et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2017; Cameselle and Gouveia, 2018; Li et al., 2019). PRBs present potential advantages over P&T in terms of lower management costs, lower energy demand, absence of external discharges, less site disturbance (Sakr et al., 2023). Furthermore, PRBs promotes the degradation of the contaminants, rather than their phase transfer.

Zero-valent iron (ZVI), activated carbon, and natural/synthetic zeolites have been widely used in PRBs for the treatment of chlorinated hydrocarbon plumes (Accardi et al., 2012; Baric et al., 2012; Piscitello et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2020). In particular, ZVI is the reactive medium most commonly employed for chlorinated ethenes and ethanes (Odziemkowski et al., 1998; Furukawa et al., 2002), although the PRB-ZVI technology is affected by some operational issues, such as the long-term performance decrease due to loss of ZVI reactivity and/or porosity reduction (Song and Carraway, 2005; Henderson and Demond, 2007). Indeed, the alkaline pH (8–9) and the presence of ferrous and ferric ions within the barrier, as a consequence of ZVI corrosion, can lead to porosity reduction, mainly due to the expansive nature of iron corrosion products. This aspect might hamper the electron transfer process, reducing the iron reactivity (Odziemkowski et al., 1998; Furukawa et al., 2002). Additionally, iron precipitation could cause pore occlusion, resulting in a greater flow velocity and reducing the treatment effectiveness, due to the decrease of the residence time within the PRB (Morrison and Bartlett, 2009; Baric et al., 2012). However, some compounds, such as chloromethane, dichloromethane and 1,2-DCA, do not undergo chemical reduction in the presence of ZVI (Song and Carraway, 2005; Henderson and Demond, 2007).

In addition to physical-chemical processes, most chlorinated solvents can be effectively degraded by biological processes carried out by bacteria. Biodegradation can occur through an oxidative (aerobic) or a reductive (anaerobic) reaction, via a direct or cometabolic pathway (Frascari et al., 2015). In direct aerobic oxidation, the chlorinated compound acts as electron donor and growth substrate for microorganisms, while oxygen is the electron acceptor. Conversely, in aerobic cometabolism, oxygenase enzymes, synthetized by microorganisms for the uptake of growth substrates, fortuitously catalyze the oxidation of the chlorinated compound. Oxidative processes require nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide - hydrogen (NADH) as a source of reducing energy, which is regenerated through the oxidation of the growth substrate. However, in aerobic cometabolism, NADH cannot be regenerated, and biodegradation continues until the available reducing energy is depleted (Van Hylckama Vlieg et al., 1996). Fig. S1 shows a schematic representation of oxidation process of the growth and cometabolic substrates mediated by monooxygenase enzyme. Generally, low-chlorinated compounds are degraded through an oxidative direct pathway; while polychlorinated compounds can be effectively degraded via reductive dechlorination (Furukawa et al., 2002). Biological reductive dechlorination (BRD) is an anaerobic multi-step reaction carried out by specialized microorganisms present in anoxic environments, such as groundwater ecosystems, in which highly chlorinated compounds are converted to less chlorinated by-products and finally to non-toxic end products, e.g., ethene and ethane (Xiao et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021; Amanat et al., 2022). BRD is an anaerobic respiratory process, called dehalorespiration, and microorganisms able to respire chlorinated compounds, utilizing them as terminal electron acceptors, are called organohalide respiring bacteria (OHRB) (Hug et al., 2013; Song et al., 2023). The reduction mechanism takes place in two stages (Fig. S2). The first stage consists in the transfer of a single electron from an electron donor to the chlorinated aliphatic compound with the removal of a chlorine atom and the consequent formation of an alkyl radical. In most cases, the alkyl radical formation is the rate-limiting process in the overall reaction. The second stage consists in a hydrogenolysis reaction, in which the alkyl radical binds a hydrogen ion to itself. BRD is an electron consuming process and is often limited by the lack of suitable electron donors resulting in an incomplete degradation and the accumulation of undesired by-products (Li et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2021; Amanat et al., 2022). Therefore, BRD can be sustained and enhanced through the addition of fermentable substrates (e.g., hydrogen, butyrate, lactate), available as a source of electron donors for microorganisms (Yu et al., 2023). The additional source of carbon and energy as a co-substrate supports bacterial growth and metabolism, and biodegradation of the target chlorinated compound is carried out by the biochemical capability of microorganisms (Gao and Gu, 2021).

To date, poly-β-hydroxybutyrate (PHB), derived from both pure and mixed microbial culture, has proven to be effective as slow-release electron donor for the BRD process (Aulenta et al., 2008; Pierro et al., 2017; Amanat et al., 2021a, 2021b, 2022). Moreover, various studies confirmed the feasibility to use PHB as reactive medium in PRBs (Baric et al., 2012, 2014; Matturro et al., 2018; Amanat et al., 2021b, 2022). In this light, a bio-PRB represents an environmental biotechnology to use in detoxifying and eliminating pollutants, and remediate contaminated aquifers (Gu, 2020). Furthermore, reactive materials in bio-PRBs provide a carbon supply for the attachment and growth of potentially biodegrading microorganisms transported in the soil water (Freidman et al., 2017). To date, there are few experimental studies in which PHB has been used as fermentable substrate to support BRD (Aulenta et al., 2005a, 2005b; Baric et al., 2012, 2014; Matturro et al., 2018; Amanat et al., 2021a, 2021b, 2022); these studies have been conducted on microcosm- or laboratory-scale, ensuring anaerobic conditions within the system, and used synthetic waters contaminated with chlorinated compounds (PCE, TCE, 1,2-DCA). This aspect, if on one hand simplified the understanding of mechanisms occurring within the system, on the other hand, did not allow to appreciate the possible issues related to the treatment of a real contaminated water, in which there are many other compounds and factors that could cause interferences.

In this context, the aim of the present study was to evaluate the feasibility of a bioremediation approach for a real groundwater contaminated by chlorinated solvents (mainly 1,2-DCA), in a column simulation of a bio-PRB, using PHB as fermentable substrate and slow-release electron donor to sustain microbial growth and BRD process. An experimental bench-scale apparatus was realized, consisting in two parallel columns, simulating an anaerobic PHB-based PRB and an aerobic bioremediation approach. Both columns were fed with real contaminated groundwater and inoculated with pre-enriched dechlorinating consortia.

The novelty of this study relies in the use of real groundwater collected from an aquifer mainly contaminated by 1,2-DCA. Our results can provide useful preliminary indications towards the evaluation of 1,2-DCA anaerobic and aerobic biodegradation pathways when treating real contaminated groundwater.

The experimental campaign had an overall duration of 180 days. During the first 90 days, enrichment cultures were set up from the groundwater contaminated by chlorinated solvents, in order to favor the autochthonous dechlorinating bacterial population. A dechlorinating bacterial consortium was enriched in presence of PHB powder, as electron donor for the BRD process, under anaerobic conditions. In parallel, an enrichment culture on 1,2-DCA was carried out from the same groundwater under aerobic conditions, in order to biostimulate oxidative processes. During the subsequent 90 days, a pilot study was carried out on a laboratory-scale plant fed with the real contaminated groundwater, inoculated with the dechlorinating bacterial consortia mentioned above.

Before being used for experimentation, the real groundwater sample was stored at 4 °C in a container hermetically sealed with no headspace, in order to limit the exposure to atmospheric oxygen, maintain anaerobic conditions and limit contaminants volatilization. The groundwater sample was contaminated by a variety of chlorinated solvents, with 1,2-DCA representing the major contaminant with a concentration of 20 mg l−1. It was also characterized by a negative redox potential, a neutral pH, high values of electrical conductivity and total dissolved solids. Table S1 shows the main physical-chemical characteristics of groundwater sample used in this study.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Set up of enrichment cultures in microcosm
ce:section.ce:para: Enrichment cultures in microcosm were set up using the real groundwater sample from the contaminated aquifer in order to enrich the autochthonous 1,2-DCA dechlorinating bacterial community. Anaerobic enrichment cultures were set up with groundwater and culture medium (Marzorati et al., 2006) (50% vol/vol), amended with 1,2-DCA 100 ppm and biostimulated with PHB powder 3.4 mM to a final volume of 12 ml into 20 ml screw cap vials in an anaerobic box under an atmosphere of filter-sterilized N2. The anaerobic cultures were incubated statically in the dark at room temperature. In parallel, aerobic enrichment cultures were set up with groundwater and culture medium (Coleman et al., 2002) and were amended with 1,2-DCA 100 ppm and a mixture of volatile hydrocarbons (1% methane, 1% ethane, 0.01% C4–C6) in a final volume of 12 ml into 20 ml screw cap vials. The aerobic cultures were incubated in the dark at room temperature on a rotary shaker. In order to confirm that 1,2-DCA degradation was carried out by microorganisms, in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions, abiotic controls were set up in parallel to the biologically active treatments (Gu, 2016) using filter-sterilized groundwater. All microcosms were prepared in triplicate. At the end of four established incubation times (0, 15, 30 and 45 days), a set of microcosms of each condition was analyzed by gas-chromatography as described in 2.4. section. After 45 days of incubation, the obtained anaerobic and aerobic dechlorinating cultures were further enriched by transferring an inoculum (10% vol/vol) into fresh culture medium for 45 more days. These consortia were used as inoculum into the column systems as described below.

Two parallel Plexiglas columns (length: 44 cm, inner diameter: 2.8 cm), namely Column A and Column B, were realized and continuously fed upward with the same contaminated groundwater sample. Column A was conceived to simulate a first PRB portion (from 0 to 22 cm) and a down-gradient aquifer (from 22 to 44 cm): the PRB portion (section 1) was filled with a mixture of silica sand and PHB (Sigma-Aldrich, CAS 29435-48-1, purity 99.9%) at 5% on a weight basis; the aquifer portion (section 2) was filled with silica sand only. Before the start-up of the experimental activity, Column A was preliminarily flushed with nitrogen gas in order to eliminate oxygen and establish anaerobic conditions. Column B was entirely filled with silica sand and was equipped with an aeration system, placed at the flow inlet, in order to ensure aerobic conditions. A 2 cm sand and coarse gravel layer was placed at the bottom of each column to homogenize the distribution of the water flow. Both columns were equipped with a sampling port placed at the middle of the column; in addition, another sampling point has been realized at the outlet of each column.

Both columns were inoculated with a dechlorinating microbial consortium previously obtained and enriched from the same 1,2-DCA contaminated groundwater. In particular, Column A was inoculated with the microbial community enriched on PHB under anoxic conditions, with the specific aim of creating a biological reactive zone where inoculated microorganisms could use PHB fermentation products as suitable electron donors for BRD. Instead, Column B was inoculated with the microbial consortium enriched on 1,2-DCA in presence of O2, with the aim of promoting bacterial aerobic oxidative (co)metabolism. In each column, 70 ml of groundwater were inoculated with 10% (vol/vol) bacterial culture at OD600 = 0.1 and left in batch conditions for one week, before starting the continuous groundwater feeding.

During the experimentation, both columns were covered and kept in the dark in order to simulate the aquifer real conditions and avoid algae formation. Throughout the entire experimental activity (90 days), groundwater was continuously pumped into the columns by two peristaltic pumps at a flow rate of 0.1 ml min−1, which corresponded to 30 h of residence time or 1.3 cm h−1 of pore water velocity. The feed water was stored in sealed bags with a capacity of about 2 l, which were periodically refilled (autonomy of about 14 days). For Column A, the bags were previously flushed with nitrogen gas to eliminate oxygen and ensure anaerobic conditions. Furthermore, in order to remove any residual dissolved oxygen in the feeding water for Column A, a deoxygenation procedure with sodium sulphite and cobalt chloride, was performed in accordance with Capodici et al. (2019). Before each bags refill, groundwater was enriched in nutrients (urea - CH4N2O: 7.5 ml in 1 l of water and potassium dihydrogen phosphate - K2HPO4: 8.6 ml in 1 l of water) in order to avoid limitations for microbial growth; nutrients were dosed according to Baric et al. (2014).
Fig. S3 shows a schematic layout and a panoramic view of both laboratory-scale column systems.

During the experimental activity, the main operational parameters, i.e., dissolved oxygen (DO), redox potential (ORP), electric conductivity (EC), and pH have been regularly measured in the sampling cell located at the outlet of both columns, by means of dedicated probes connected to a multimeter (WTW 3340).

Liquid samples were periodically (every 14 days) collected at the inlet, at the middle (corresponding to a retention time of 900 min) and at the outlet of each column (corresponding to a retention time of 1800 min). In Column A, where the middle point of sampling corresponded with the outlet of PRB, the aim was to monitor physical-chemical parameters of the influent water, PHB fermentation in terms of acetate production, and BRD progress in terms of 1,2-DCA removal. In Column B, the aim was to monitor oxidative degradative reactions in terms of 1,2-DCA removal. In detail, 1,2-DCA concentration in both enrichment cultures in microcosm and in column systems was measured by headspace-gaschromatography/mass spectrometry using the 7000C GC/MS Triple Quad GC/MS System, equipped with the column Agilent 19091S–433UI; helium was used as carrier gas, oven temperature was set at 240 °C and injection temperature was 270 °C. In Column A, Volatile Fatty Acids (VFAs) were analyzed by ion chromatography (DIONEX ICS-1100) according to APAT IRSA CNR 4020 method.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of the microbial communities by Illumina Miseq 16S rRNA gene sequencing
ce:section.ce:para: The microbial communities of the two portions (section 1 and 2, respectively) of both columns were characterized using high throughput 16S rRNA gene amplicons sequencing. At the end of the experimental period, samples of sand were recovered from both sections of Columns A and B. Metagenomic DNA was extracted from 0.5 g of each sample using the Fast DNA™ SPIN Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, Solon, OH, USA) following manufacturer's instructions. Purity and concentration of extracted DNA were assessed using a NanoDROP ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). As already reported (Corsino et al., 2022), metagenomic DNA obtained from each sample was used as template to amplify bacterial and archaeal V3–V4 hypervariable region of the 16S rRNA gene using primers Pro341F (5′-CCTACGGGNBGCASCAG-3′) and Pro805R (5′-GACTACNVGGGTATCTAATCC-3′); the amplicons sequencing was carried out using Illumina-MiSeq® platform; reads filtering and denoising were performed using Qiime2 tools version 2019.4 and taxonomy was assigned using trained Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) at 99% from Green Genes database version 13–8. 16S rRNA gene sequences obtained in this study were deposited in GenBank (NCBI) within the PRJNA939953 Bioproject (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/PRJNA939953).

Gas-chromatographic analysis conducted on anaerobic and aerobic enrichment cultures after 45 days incubation during the preliminary experimental study revealed a removal of 1,2-DCA of about 90% in the PHB-biostimulated anaerobic microcosms, and of 100% in the aerobic microcosms. A decrease of 1,2-DCA concentration was also observed in anaerobic/aerobic abiotic controls, but to a lesser extent (30% and 70%, respectively) (Fig. S4), indicating that 1,2-DCA could be partially degraded by abiotic reactions. However, the almost total removal of 1,2-DCA in biotic microcosms indicated that biodegradation mechanisms also existed, and predominated in anaerobic conditions, thus highlighting that a dechlorinating community was enriched in microcosm in both conditions. The obtained dechlorinating consortia were further enriched and used to inoculate the two columns of the continuous-flow experimental apparatus.

As expected, the two columns showed a different behavior throughout experiments. Fig. 1 shows physical-chemical parameters variation during the continuous-flow experimental campaign within both columns. Fig. 1a reports the trend profile of DO concentration. In Column A, DO concentration was always equal to zero confirming the establishment of anaerobic conditions into the column, excepting a short period (from day 60 to day 78) when a sudden increase of the DO concentration was observed. This increase could be likely due to an improper water-bag storage. In contrast, in Column B, DO concentration measured at the outlet of the system, was significantly high, thus confirming aerobic conditions into the column. Interestingly, a decreasing trend of DO concentration in Column B during experiments was observed, probably due to biotic oxygen consumption. DO behavior within the two columns was confirmed by ORP values measured throughout experiments and shown in Fig. 1c. In particular, in Column A ORP always showed negative values, excepting the short period corresponding to the increase of DO concentration. Also, ORP negative values confirmed anaerobic conditions within Column A. Conversely, in Column B ORP always showed positive values, thus indicating aerobic conditions within the system. EC remained almost constant over time in both columns, with higher values observed in Column A compared to Column B (Fig. 1b). Regarding pH (Fig. 1d), it showed an increasing trend in Column A. This trend could be explained by a balance between two opposite phenomena occurring simultaneously into Column A: on one hand, PHB hydrolysis produced acetate, leading to a pH decrease, while on the other hand, acetate consumption by microorganisms caused an increase in alkalinity. It is probable that, from a kinetic point of view, acetate consumption overwhelmed production, thus determining a pH increasing trend. In Column B, pH remained constant around 7.6.

ce:section.ce:section-title: PHB fermentation and acetate production in Column A

ce:section.ce:para: Referring to Column A, 1,2-DCA was degraded until reaching a concentration close to the standard limit imposed by Legislative Decree No 152/06 (1,2-DCA = 6 μg l−1; CSC - contamination threshold concentration = 3 μg l−1) on the 60th experimental day, and it was below the instrument detection limit after 75 days of operation. On the contrary, in Column B, although the significant 1,2-DCA removal (98%), the degradation rate was lower and 1,2-DCA concentration at the end of the experiment was considerably higher than CSC (1,2-DCA = 324 μg l−1). Moreover, as abiotic reactions could significantly contribute to 1,2-DCA removal in Column B, as assumed for the aerobic abiotic microcosm, the biological aerobic degradation seems to be less efficient. Fig. 4 shows 1,2-DCA concentration trend along the two columns. Furthermore, Fig. S5 shows the normalized trend of the effluent 1,2-DCA for the two columns during the experimental period. In both columns very low values of normalized 1,2-DCA were found, with a general decreasing trend, confirming a high 1,2-DCA (bio)degradation, with removal efficiencies always higher than 90%. In Column A, after 75 experimental days, an almost complete removal of the 1,2-DCA was obtained, with an efficiency close to 100%. The maximum removal efficiency observed in Column B, on the other hand, was approximately 98%.

Microbial biomass within both columns was estimated as total double strand extracted DNA (dsDNA) referred to one gram of sand (Catania et al., 2022). Columns A and B had a similar biomass content that was higher in section 1 with respect to section 2 for both columns (Table 1 ). Illumina MiSeq 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed on the metagenomic DNA extracted from the silica sand samples from Columns A and B in order to detect and identify the bacterial communities and to verify the presence of microbes involved in BRD and direct or cometabolic oxidation of chlorinated solvents.

The summary of Illumina sequencing output is reported in Table 1. Clustering of 16S rRNA gene sequences at 99% similarity led to a similar number of OTUs in the two sections from Column A (143 for section 1 and 131 for section 2), and a slightly higher number of OTUs in Column B. The clusters were taxonomically identified using GreenGenes database version 13–8.

The histograms in Fig. 5 show the composition of the two microbial consortia at phylum (Fig. 5a), family (Fig. 5b) and genus (Fig. 5c) taxonomic level. Taxonomic groups with relative abundance greater than 1% were taken into consideration. The most represented phyla in both columns were Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, followed by Bacteroidetes and Tenericutes. Column A was dominated by Firmicutes (50% and 64%, in section 1 and 2 respectively) followed by Tenericutes (25% and 1%). Conversely, Column B was dominated by Proteobacteria (57% in both sections), followed by Firmicutes (28% and 14%).

At family level, Column A was mainly composed of Peptococcaceae (23% and 53%, in section 1 and 2 respectively) and Acidaminobacteraceae (19% and 8%), and, to a lesser extent, Pelobacteraceae (8% in section 2), Desulfovibrionaceae (3% and 2%) and Syntrophaceae (2% and 1%). Members of these families are almost exclusively obligate anaerobes, confirming that anaerobic conditions were established throughout Column A (Fig. 1). Peptococcaceae were represented mainly by Desulfosporosinus (3% and 15%, in section 1 and 2 respectively), while Acidaminobacteraceae were totally represented by Fusibacter, which was the most abundant identified genus in section 1. In at least one section of Column A the families Pseudomonadaceae (4.5% in section 2), Comamonadaceae (3% in section 1) and Desulfuromonadaceae (1.5% in section 2) were also identified. Five out of the total detected families, namely Peptococcaceae, Desulfovibrionaceae, Desulfuromonadaceae, Syntrophaceae and Comamonadaceae, include known OHRB genera (Molenda et al., 2020; Türkowsky et al., 2018).

In Column B, Proteobacteria were mainly made up of families Legionellaceae (22%) and Comamonadaceae (6%) in section 1, Comamonadaceae (14%), Pseudomonadaceae (11%), Rhodocyclaceae (10%) and Desulfuromonadaceae (5%) in section 2, and Enterobacteriaceae (4%) in both sections. Firmicutes were mainly made up of Peptococcaceae (including the unidentified phylotype EtOH8) in both sections (24.5% in section 1 and 10% in section 2). Legionellaceae are aerobic Gram-negative bacilli that are found mainly in aqueous environments (Edelstein and Lück, 2015); they were probably present in the groundwater used to feed the columns and enriched in Column B taking advantage of oxygen. Beyond aerobic Legionellaceae, Comamonadaceae and Pseudomonadaceae, Column B also hosts facultative and anaerobic bacteria (i.e., Enterobacteriaceae, Peptococcaceae and Desulfuromonadaceae). The presence of facultative and anaerobic bacteria suggests the formation of micro-oxygen depletion zones inside Column B, probably due to aerobic microbial consumption, in accordance to the detected decrease of DO (Fig. 1). Anaerobic Peptococcaceae were mainly represented by Desulfosporosinus (19% and 9%, in section 1 and 2 respectively). The genera identified within Comamonadaceae were Delftia (just over 4% in both sections) and Hydrogenophaga (1% in section 1 and 5% in section 2). Pseudomonadaceae were totally represented by the genus Pseudomonas (2.5% and 10.5%, in section 1 and 2 respectively), that is the most abundant genus in section 2. Among families hosted in Column B, Comamonadaceae, Pseudomonadaceae, Peptococcaceae and Desulfuromonadaceae include known degraders of chlorinated solvents (Bertolini et al., 2021; Dolinová et al., 2017).

The biodegradation of 1,2-DCA observed in the preliminary microcosm test, more efficiently under anaerobic conditions with respect to aerobic ones, highlighted that a dechlorinating microbial community was enriched from the autochthonous microbiota of the contaminated groundwater in both conditions. Our results demonstrate that both biological pathways (anaerobic BRD and aerobic direct/cometabolic oxidation) are feasible alternatives for 1,2-DCA removal from contaminated groundwater (Frascari et al., 2015; Amanat et al., 2022) once the presence of a biodegradation potential has been established.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 1,2-DCA biodegradation supported by PHB fermentation in anaerobic Column A
ce:section.ce:para: Results from Column A showed that PHB powder was effectively hydrolyzed and used as substrate by the anaerobic enriched culture of autochthonous groundwater microorganisms that converted it into acetate (which was accumulated up to 267 mg l−1 after 90 experimentation days). The rapid fermentation was determined not only by the favorable conditions established into the system, but also by the high specific surface of the biopolymer itself. In particular, along Column A, the highest acetate concentration was observed at the end of PRB section, rather than at the exit of the column. This is probably due because PHB hydrolysis took place in the reactive portion of the column, resulting in the production of acetate, while in the aquifer section acetate was consumed and used as growth substrate by microorganisms. However, the amount of acetate deriving from PHB fermentation was sufficient to sustain an efficient and prolonged reductive dechlorination activity in the column, as demonstrated by the complete 1,2-DCA removal. So PHB, acting as slow-release electron donor in the form of acetate, can be effectively used to support a long-term reductive dechlorination microbial metabolism, allowing the removal of the chlorinated contaminant and confirming the effectiveness of anaerobic BRD pathway for 1,2-DCA biodegradation (Baric et al., 2014).

Column B showed a slightly lower 1,2-DCA removal efficiency (98%). In this case, presumed abiotic reactions also acted in 1,2-DCA removal, while the biodegradation of the chlorinated compound was probably mediated by the establishment of both aerobic and anaerobic dechlorination pathways, as suggested by DO and redox potential values achieved during the experimental campaign. Aerobic biodegradation of 1,2-DCA has been observed in previous studies, in which it has been shown that 1,2-DCA can be degraded both by direct oxidation and by oxidative cometabolism (Munro et al., 2017).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Microbial communities in the columns and their proposed role in 1,2-DCA biodegradation
ce:section.ce:para: The microbial consortia established in Columns A and B, analyzed at the end of the experimental period, derived from the autochthonous microbial community of the groundwater used to feed both columns and from the two 1,2-DCA dechlorinating consortia previously enriched in microcosm from the same groundwater and used as inoculum in both columns. In particular, Column A inoculum was made up of a microbial consortium enriched on PHB under anaerobic conditions, while Column B was inoculated with a microbial consortium enriched on 1,2-DCA under aerobic conditions. The microbial communities of Columns A and B showed quite similar profiles at phylum level, although the relative abundances of the identified taxa varied between the two columns and between sections within each column. Since the columns were fed with the same groundwater sample, the difference in the composition of the two final communities is to be attributed to the different microbial inocula used for the two columns and to the different physical-chemical conditions established in each column, referring in particular to the presence of PHB and DO concentrations.

In Column A, the degradation of PHB was evidenced by acetate formation and by microbial biomass proliferation. Anaerobic conditions in the presence of PHB favored the enrichment of fermentative/sulfate reducing bacteria. Indeed, the most abundant genera, Desulfosporosinus and Fusibacter, are both sulfate and thiosulfate reducers and they have also a fermentative metabolism that could be responsible for acetate production from PHB (Hippe and Stackebrandt, 2015; Ravot et al., 2015). In particular, Desulfosporosinus, a strictly anaerobic spore forming sulfate-reducing bacterium, can produce acetate as fermentation end product (Hippe and Stackebrandt, 2015). Moreover, sulfate reducing bacteria (SRB) are known to be involved also in biodegradation of aromatic and chlorinated hydrocarbons (Dutta et al., 2022) and Desulfosporosinus, in particular, includes PCE-degrading species (Spring and Rosenzweig, 2006), such as D. meridiei (Robertson et al., 2001). Desulfosporosinus was recently detected as the most abundant active genus, resident in an organohalide polluted groundwater underneath a landfill stimulated with molasses (Bertolini et al., 2021). Also, the genus Fusibacter could have a role as both fermenting and OHRB agent responsible for both acetate production from the degradation of PHB and dehalogenation of 1,2-DCA (Ravot et al., 1999). Although both genera have been described as OHRB, the specific role of Desulfosporosinus and Fusibacter in 1,2-DCA dehalogenation is observed here for the first time; further investigations are needed to confirm it. Beyond members of Peptococcaceae, also members of Desulfovibrionaceae, Desulfuromonadaceae, Syntrophaceae and Comamonadaceae, detected in Column A at lower abundance, include known dehalogenating species (Türkowsky et al., 2018; Molenda et al., 2020), which could be involved in 1,2-DCA biodegradation in our experimental system. Surprisingly the most well-known OHRB genera (i.e., Dehalococcoides, Dehalogenimonas, Dehalobacter, Desulfitobacterium) were not detected in Column A, but it is worth to note that a large part of the reads could not be assigned at genus level suggesting that other dehalogenating taxa could be present. According to microbial community composition, the most probable mechanism for 1,2-DCA biodegradation in Column A is reductive dechlorination carried out by SRB and enhanced by fermentation products from PHB degradation.

Unlike Column A, alternate aerobic/anoxic microsites in Column B enriched the consortium with a less abundant and more diverse microbial community, composed mainly of aerobic chemoorganotrophs and anaerobic fermentative/sulfate reducing bacteria. Among identified families, Pseudomonadaceae, Comamonadaceae, Peptococcaceae and Desulfuromonadaceae include known degraders of chlorinated solvents (Dolinová et al., 2017; Bertolini et al., 2021). One of the most abundant genera in section 1 was Desulfosporosinus, already described referring to Column A. While the most abundant genus in section 2 was Pseudomonas that includes known hydrocarbon degraders and species able to carry out (co)metabolic oxidation of chlorinated solvents (Alvarez-Cohen and Speitel, 2001). Pseudomonas sp. strain DCA1, for example, can utilize 1,2-DCA as sole carbon and energy source (Hage et al., 2001), suggesting that members of this genus could have a pivotal role in 1,2-DCA degradation in Column B by both direct and cometabolic oxidation. Also, the genera Delftia and Hydrogenophaga, detected in Column B at lower abundance, could be responsible of 1,2-DCA biodegradation. It has been reported that many species of Delftia live in anoxic-aerobic environments, and they could dehalogenate and degrade halogenated aromatic compounds, such as diuron, 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetate, chlorophenoxy herbicides, trifluoroacetate and 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxybenzoate (Zhang et al., 2019). Hydrogenophaga includes aerobic chemorganotrophic or chemolithoautotrophic bacteria and some strains have demonstrated the ability to aerobically degrade chlorinated compounds, such as polychlorinated biphenyls (Lambo and Patel, 2007). However, further investigations should assess the ability of these genera to dehalogenate also 1,2-DCA. According to Column B microbial composition, 1,2-DCA biodegradation in the imposed aerobic experimental system could mostly occur by an aerobic oxidative pathway, both direct and cometabolic, and could be supported by anaerobic reductive dechlorination processes. Our experimental approach demonstrates the feasibility to detect and exploit the biodegradation potential of the autochthonous bacterial population of a contaminated site as a starting point for an in situ bioremediation strategy. We demonstrated that preliminary biostimulation in microcosm testing different biostimulating conditions, allows to obtain enriched dehalogenating consortia that are effective at removing the contaminant from a real contaminated groundwater in a laboratory-scale PRB trial. This approach allows a more effective intervention of bioremediation by stimulation in the field once the best conditions for dehalogenation are identified for each specific contaminated site.

In the present study, aerobic and anaerobic biostimulation and bioaugmentation treatments were investigated for the bioremediation of a real groundwater mainly polluted by 1,2-DCA, by exploiting the biodegradation potential of the autochthonous bacterial communities. We demonstrated that both aerobic and anaerobic dehalogenating activity can be stimulated effectively in the same site and that the two obtained enriched consortia were composed of partially/putatively known dehalogenating bacteria. Anaerobic 1,2-DCA degradation was mainly carried out by fermentative/sulfate reducing bacteria stimulated by acetate derived from PHB fermentation in Column A. Conversely, mainly aerobic (co)metabolic oxidation by aerobic chemoorganotrophs occurred in Column B. Our results highlight that a variety of biological processes can be effectively stimulated for the remediation of aquifers contaminated by chlorinated solvents and also other xenobiotics, promoting the application of more environmentally sustainable remediation approaches based on the natural biodegradation potential of autochthonous microrganisms.
